name: Drafting a Manuscript
title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript is the work of turning a research project into a structured document that can be read, reviewed, and cited. It covers the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, references, and supplementary material, along with figures, tables, and any required statements. The draft must make an argument, place that argument against prior work, and give enough detail for another researcher to evaluate and reproduce the study. It is distinct from data collection and from formal peer review, though it is written with both in mind. This site's library holds 135 research papers, which shows the scale of prior work a new draft may need to address.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A manuscript is usually drafted in a word processor or in LaTeX, often through a collaborative platform such as Overleaf. Reference managers like Zotero or EndNote hold the bibliography, and BibTeX or a citation style file applies the venue's format. Version control, whether Git or a cloud document history, helps track changes across authors and reviewers. Most journals provide templates and require submission through their own manuscript system, which then handles metadata, file checks, and reviewer routing. A preprint server may be used alongside or before that submission, depending on the venue's policy.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with an outline that maps each section to the claims it must support and the evidence it will cite. Authors draft in passes, writing the methods and results first, then the introduction and discussion, and leaving the abstract for last. Figures and tables are built to stand alone, with captions that state what was measured and what the reader should notice. Citations are checked against the original sources, and the draft is revised for clarity, scope, and consistency with reporting guidelines. Internal review, coauthor sign off, and a final check of data and code availability statements are part of the same process, and the site's 11795 claims extracted from research works show how granular this claim to evidence mapping can become.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in drafting center on authorship, originality, and provenance. Authors agree on order and contributions, disclose conflicts of interest and funding, and secure permission for any reused figures or data. The draft is expected to avoid plagiarism and self-plagiarism, and it is not submitted elsewhere unless the venue allows it. Copyright transfer or licensing terms are set by the venue, and preprint or open access choices can affect those terms. Provenance is supported by accurate citations, data availability statements, code repositories, and clear disclosure of any AI assistance used in writing.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting is moving toward more structured, machine readable manuscripts that link claims to evidence, data, and code. Registered reports and preprints shift some review before or alongside drafting, and open peer review makes the draft a more public object. Persistent identifiers, contributor role taxonomies, and reporting checklists are becoming part of the submission package. AI writing assistants are changing how drafts are produced, while venues are adding disclosure rules and detection checks. The direction is toward drafts that are checked against structured claim records rather than only a reference list.
